title: Tamsin and the Inventory
premise: Theo Sandoval, a piano tuner who reads a house's history through its pipes and radiators, has spent thirty years perfecting the smile that ends conversations. When the Sandoval family home goes up for auction, she returns to tune the estate's ancient upright and discovers the radiators still hold the sound of the night her brother disappeared—and that every relative's version of that night protects someone else. As the auction date closes in, Theo must decide whether to voice the question the whole family arranged itself around: what really happened to Milo? In the end, she speaks the truth at the auction itself, losing the house but gaining a family rebuilt on honesty rather than silence.
about_author: Yara Dunmore is a former building conservator who spent a decade cataloguing historic houses before turning to fiction full-time. She writes from a converted schoolhouse in coastal Maine, where she claims she can still hear what the walls remember.

chapters.title: The Tuner's Ear
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. She tunes a stranger's piano in a stranger's house, narrating how she hears buildings—the hum of old wiring, the grief in a radiator. Establishes her gift and her practiced invisibility. Emotional beat: competent solitude masking loneliness.

chapters.title: Notice of Sale
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. A certified letter arrives: the Sandoval house on Corliss Street will be auctioned in six weeks. Her aunt Renata calls with instructions to collect 'her things' quietly. Beat: dread sharpened into resolve; Theo decides to go back once, briefly.

chapters.title: Corliss Street
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. She walks the empty childhood home, tuning the parlor upright as an excuse to stay. The radiators groan with remembered sounds—Milo's laugh, a slammed door, rain the night he vanished at seventeen. Beat: the past made physical; grief reawakened.

chapters.title: The Family Arrangement
chapters.summary: Renata's POV. Flashback-tinged chapter showing how the family divided itself after Milo's disappearance: who got which silence, which story, which room never mentioned. Beat: reveals the machinery of enforced forgetting Theo was raised inside.

chapters.title: Aunt Renata's Ledger
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Sorting the attic, Theo finds Renata's meticulous household ledger with a torn page dated the week Milo disappeared. Renata catches her holding it and, for the first time, looks afraid. Beat: first crack in the family's sealed story.

chapters.title: Cousin Dee Returns
chapters.summary: Dee's POV. Theo's cousin arrives to claim furniture, all charm and hurry. Dee remembers more than she admits about the night Milo left—but she owes Renata everything. Beat: alliance offered and withheld; loyalty shown as debt.

chapters.title: What the Radiators Say
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Working alone at night, Theo maps the house's sounds room by room, reconstructing the night of Milo's disappearance: two voices arguing, a car door, footsteps that went down but never came up. Beat: the mystery takes shape; Theo can no longer pretend not to know there is something to know.

chapters.title: Uncle Ambrose's Version
chapters.summary: Ambrose's POV. The eldest uncle gives Theo his polished account—Milo ran off, no blame, case closed—and we see him rehearsing it like scripture. Beat: sympathy for the keeper of the official story; his certainty reads as cost.

chapters.title: The Appraiser
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. An appraiser values the house and its contents; the upright piano is flagged as nearly worthless, which stings Theo into bidding intentions she hasn't confessed. Beat: stakes become concrete—a deadline, a price, a rival for the house itself.

chapters.title: Dee's Debt
chapters.summary: Dee's POV. Renata reminds Dee of the loan that saved her business, making clear what silence costs. Dee almost tells Theo about the second car in the driveway that night. Beat: loyalty vs. truth dramatized inside one character; she chooses silence again, hating it.

chapters.title: The Torn Page
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo matches the ledger's missing page to carbon paper in Renata's desk: an entry recording money paid out the morning after Milo vanished—to whom, the name is smudged. Beat: the story shifts from 'what happened' to 'who paid'; suspicion enters the family.

chapters.title: Confrontation in the Kitchen
chapters.summary: Alternating Theo/Renata. Theo asks directly; Renata answers with fury and, underneath it, exhaustion: 'You want the truth or you want the family? You cannot price both.' Beat: midpoint rupture; Theo is threatened with exile from the only family she has.

chapters.title: The Neighbor Across the Street
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. A longtime neighbor, outside the family's arrangement, offers the view from across the street: she saw the car, saw who drove it, and has kept quiet out of kindness for thirty years. Beat: an outsider's witness breaks the insider seal; hope and fear together.

chapters.title: Ambrose Breaks
chapters.summary: Ambrose's POV. Confronted with Marisol's account, Ambrose admits the driver was their father, already dying, and that the family protected a dead man's name by burying a living boy's question. Beat: confession as relief and ruin; the official story collapses.

chapters.title: What Happened to Milo
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Piecing ledger, testimony, and the radiators' record, Theo reconstructs it: Milo wasn't taken—he left, aided by their father, after a fight over Theo herself; he wrote once, and Renata intercepted the letter. Beat: devastating clarity; the question answered opens a worse one—where is Milo now?

chapters.title: The Letter
chapters.summary: Renata's POV. Renata surrenders the unopened letter she kept for three decades, explaining her logic: returning it would have meant admitting everything. Beat: antagonist becomes the story's most wounded figure; forgiveness becomes possible but not yet given.

chapters.title: Finding Milo
chapters.summary: Theo and Dee's POV, alternating. Using the letter's postmark, they trace Milo to a town two states away; he is alive, wary, tuning pianos himself. Beat: reunion deferred by fear; found-family theme inverted—blood family must earn what strangers gave him.

chapters.title: Eve of Auction
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. The family gathers the night before the sale, everyone knowing, no one speaking. Theo rehearses what she'll say and realizes the house was never the inheritance—the truth was. Beat: quiet before climax; resolve crystallizes.

chapters.title: The Auction
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. At the podium, with the gavel poised, Theo stands and tells the whole room—the neighbors, the bidders, the family—what happened to Milo. The house sells to a stranger; Renata walks out; Dee stays. Beat: climax; truth spoken at maximum cost.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. The family scatters and regroups: Ambrose feels lighter, Renata refuses calls, Dee moves toward Theo. Theo, houseless by choice, sits in her van outside the sold home listening to its new silence. Beat: desolation and strange freedom entwined.

chapters.title: Two Pianos
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Milo comes to her workshop; they tune a battered upright together without discussing the past, letting the work say what words can't. He agrees to come to Sunday dinner—not forgiveness, but presence. Beat: reconciliation begun, not completed; earned warmth.

chapters.title: The New Arrangement
chapters.summary: Theo's POV, coda. One year later: a rented house with honest radiators, Sunday dinners with Dee, Milo, even a fragile truce with Renata. Theo tunes a client's piano and lets the conversation continue past her old ending smile. Beat: belonging rebuilt on truth; the invisible woman, visible at last.
